quote: You get the balance sheet and the guy who's running it, and you better be happy with both of them.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Peter Foreman's line to him in 1983; the base of the three filters.

quote: We say the three things we want a large discount to underlying business value. So, we try to make a guess based on what we think the company could be worth seven years from now, discounted back to today.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Filter 1: value estimate seven years out, discounted back.

quote: We'd like to buy at something in the 60s cents on the dollar, what we think the business is actually worth.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Entry price versus own estimate of business value.

quote: to us, worth means like what's the maximum price an allcash buyer could pay to own the whole business and still earn an adequate return on investment.
speaker: Bill Nygren
measure: maximum price an all-cash buyer could pay
note: Definition of business value.

quote: And if we can get it at 60% of that, we're very very happy.
speaker: Bill Nygren

quote: The second thing is we want the combination of dividend income and expected per share value growth to at least match what we expect for the S&P 500.
speaker: Bill Nygren
measure: dividend yield plus expected per-share value growth
note: Filter 2; guards against value traps.

quote: We'd like companies where that combination is eight or 9% at a minimum.
speaker: Bill Nygren
measure: dividend yield plus expected per-share value growth
note: He gives S&P yield just under 2% plus 6 or 7% earnings growth as the comparison.

quote: it could be an Altria that pays out a yield that's about 9% and isn't expected to grow earnings or it could be an Alphabet that doesn't pay much of a dividend but is expected to grow faster than that.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Altria (high yield, no growth) and Alphabet (growth) both fit the second filter.

quote: We don't care which form the return comes in. But the reason we want that is value investing can sometimes lead you to these structurally disadvantaged companies whose best days are in the rearview mirror
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Return can come as yield or growth; the test aims at structurally disadvantaged firms.

quote: We don't want to be buying those kinds of value traps because we want to take a very long-term time horizon
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Avoid value traps whose business value declines.

quote: And then thirdly, we want like everybody, we want exceptional management. But to us that exceptional largely means that they are aligned with outside shareholders in having a goal of maximizing intermediate to long-term per share business value.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Filter 3.

quote: we want to avoid the companies that don't use a denominator and just are trying to grow their size.
speaker: Bill Nygren
measure: growth in size rather than per-share value
note: Avoid managers who build size not per-share value.

quote: our average holding period tends to be 5 to seven years.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Reason: management decisions over that time frame (divisions, buybacks, acquisitions) drive returns.

quote: You really want that combination of a company that's undervalued and an exceptional management team that's focused on maximizing long-term per share value.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Cheap alone or good management alone is not enough.

quote: figure out who the people are you really want to invest with and then look to see if you can justify the stock as being cheap enough to invest with them.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Lou Simpson's way of ordering the two tests (management first); he concludes you need both.

quote: I don't ever want to hear you say another word about quality of management until you've seen a hundred of them.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Peter Foreman after an IPO road show early in his career.

quote: After you've seen a hundred management teams, you can start to tell who's the top decile, which are the ones that are really side by side with the shareholders only focusing on maximizing long-term per share value
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Judging management needs many meetings.

quote: And if they make the company bigger, they'll make more money. and they pursue growth paths that don't really add per share value.
speaker: Bill Nygren
measure: growth paths not adding per-share value
note: The weaker end of the management spectrum.

quote: my role in most of the management meetings was to try to get them off script and I didn't want our analysts to be the ones doing that because sometimes that could harm the relationship.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: His role after becoming director of research around 1990.

quote: And I said, "What's so great about a three-legged stool?"
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Chemical company wanting an acquisition; he questioned its assumption.

quote: getting him to defend something that no one had ever second-gued. Basically got him to close the presentation book and talk to us, like just a one-on-one discussion.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Lesson: get managers off the pitch book.

quote: we learn so much more about why people think they're successful, what motivates them, what their goals are if we can get them to close the pitch book and just talk to us.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Goal in every management meeting.

quote: We don't want you making a presentation to us. Talk about what matters to you.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: What they ask of management teams.

quote: Talk about how you're going to judge success or failure. Talk about how you motivate people and all the numbers that you use to fill in your models.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Questions put to the CEO; figures can come from investor relations.

quote: So somehow you have to be able to filter down all that information to what's really going to matter to your investment decision.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Why a distilled set of principles helps.

quote: you'd try to understand what the business was worth and then only consider investing in the stock if it sold at a significant discount to your estimate of business value.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Framework he took from Ben Graham.

quote: that kind of getting something for free aspect of value investing is something that's still part of our process at Harris Associates today.
speaker: Bill Nygren
measure: price to cash or asset value
note: Cited after his school paper on National Presto selling below cash value.

quote: I wrote about National Presto, the small appliance maker out of Oaklair, Wisconsin that was selling below its cash value.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: School project; lesson: getting something for free is still part of the process.

quote: I've always felt that you're maximizing your chance of success in investing if you behave the same way as an investor as you do in the rest of your life.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: He ties his bargain-hunting temperament to growing up shopping specials.

quote: I knew that wasn't my personality to find something that was great, dream about how much better it might be a decade from now.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Why growth books (Phil Fisher) did not suit him.

quote: I mean by its nature we're we're buying stuff other people are punting and giving up on.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Value investing buys what others give up on.

quote: So you have to be comfortable taking a position that isn't in the majority.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Temperament needed for value investing.

quote: everything we do as an investor is you're looking at an uncertain future and a range of possible outcomes and you're trying to assign probabilities and you're looking to capitalize on those where you've got a different view of the possible outcomes than the average investor does.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Investing as probabilities over outcomes.

quote: I think back at that time, lots of highquality, stable businesses were selling at four or five times earnings.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Late 1970s; he put student-loan money into such stocks rather than a money market fund.

quote: And I didn't know how you could be a fundamental investor if you didn't understand accounting.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Why he studied accounting.

quote: Michael's use of variant perception is why Harris Associates adopted a devil's advocate review.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Michael Steinhardt's practice, adopted by Harris.

quote: Whenever we have an analyst presenting a new idea to us, somebody else takes the challenge of spending a couple days on that stock, reading the best short reports that they can find on it, and presenting to us why we shouldn't buy the stock.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Devil's advocate review of every new idea.

quote: We also do that with names that have been on our approved list for multiple years.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Devil's advocate review also for names long on the list.

quote: We're a very datadriven organization and we found out one of the areas over time we tended to get sloppy in was the names that had sat on our approved list for four or five years.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Lesson: stale holdings get sloppy review; led to a devil's advocate review after a year.

quote: But we try to challenge that by requiring a devil's advocate review after something's been on our approved list for more than a year that somebody comes to the table basically presenting a short argument on that same security.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Review trigger for names on the approved list.

quote: it helps us understand how we differ from the market and our expectations and helps us know what the signposts are to tell if we're right or the other side of the argument is right.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Purpose of the devil's advocate review.

quote: If you think about our basic approach, buying at 60 cents on the dollar, selling at 90, and the business growing the same as the S&P during the 5 years we hold it.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Buy at 60, sell at 90 of estimated value; arithmetic of the edge.

quote: the reality has been more like two to 300 basis points after you add back the cost, the expense ratio for the fund. So our correct ratio is something like 25 30%.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: His own record: excess return and a hit rate of 25 to 30% on forecasts.

quote: it makes it so important that we figure out as fast as we can the names that we're wrong on and get those out of the portfolio and get the capital recycled into the names where there's a better probability that we are successful that our hypothesis is correct.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Reason for the mistake protocol.

quote: We want to be very patient when the stock market isn't acting right and very impatient when the business isn't performing the way we expect it to.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Patient on price, impatient on fundamentals.

quote: reviews on all of our existing holdings where analysts are are expected to review them at least annually
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Analyst review frequency.

quote: to target those reviews toward points in time that are actionoriented.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Reviews timed around adding, trimming or a change in the hypothesis.

quote: we want the analyst to show why we believe the stock is cheap, why we're comfortable the value is going to grow, and why this is a management team we're comfortable investing with.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: What every written new idea must show; matches the three filters.

quote: everyone at the meeting is trying to present an argument why the analyst might be wrong.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Weekly investment meeting for a new idea.

quote: three of our investment leaders uh who form our stock selection group will vote on whether or not that stock should be on the approved list.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Approved list by majority vote of the stock selection group.

quote: it has to go through the process, be approved by the committee, and then put on the list before we can consider adding it to a portfolio.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Even long-term portfolio managers cannot buy off the approved list.

quote: Our list has about a 100 names on it that would be eligible for the Oakmark fund.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Size of the approved list for the Oakmark fund.

quote: That means a big business in the 250 largest sales, net income, or shareholders equity.
speaker: Bill Nygren
measure: rank by sales, net income or shareholders equity
note: Size test for the Oakmark fund's eligible universe.

quote: does this name add something to our portfolio? Is it cheaper? Is it a diversifier? Why somebody thinks that it should be added to the portfolio?
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Questions at the buy decision for portfolio fit.

quote: a two out of three vote in that group determines if it goes into the portfolio or not.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Portfolio entry decided by two of three leaders.

quote: this is an easy business to pursue to a gambler's ruin kind of outcome where you make a bad decision on one company and you think you can uh kind of make up for it by double waiting the next decision
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: A group process makes this hard to do.

quote: if I've got a buddy that says Nvidia is a great stock, but I can't put it into a value framework, it's virtually impossible for me to get that into our portfolio here.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Nvidia: no purchase without fit to the value framework.

quote: we think rapid identification of mistakes and getting capital redeployed into something where we have a higher probability of success is one of the keys to our long-term success.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Why the mistake protocol exists.

quote: we think about mistakes as direction neutral. A mistake is when you don't get a forecast right. uh it's just as much a mistake if the company comes in way above your forecast as if it comes in way below
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Mistake protocol, first part.

quote: we define mistakes in terms of company fundamentals not stock price.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Mistake protocol, second part.

quote: we want the path of least resistance to be our mistakes exit the portfolio rather than mistakes linger.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Goal of the mistake protocol.

quote: if I don't know enough to buy it then I don't know enough for it to stay in the portfolio.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Against treating ignorance as a defence of the status quo.

quote: at the first sign of a mistake and think of that as fundamentals deviating 10 to 15% from what the analyst had projected, we asked for an immediate review in front of the stock selection group
speaker: Bill Nygren
measure: deviation of fundamentals from analyst projection
note: Trigger for the first mistake review.

quote: We've looked at companies where we've made one mistake, two mistake, three mistakes, and they're the likelihood of an additional mistake is always higher after first mistakes.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Finding from their own data.

quote: We've checked that on our own data, and at least for us, that's that's rarely true.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Checked claim: a stock falling more than value estimate means a better buy.

quote: Usually, that mistake is a signal that future mistakes are more likely.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Why shortfalls are not treated as buying chances.

quote: if anyone on the stock selection group wants to recommend the name get removed from the list, they can recommend that and there'll be a vote.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: After the first review.

quote: If there's a follow-up mistake, the typical process is to immediately require a devil's advocate review.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Second shortfall step.

quote: start at square one and meet with the management team again, preferably in their offices and uh get us to recommmit to a hypothesis that we think is strong enough that if we didn't own the stock,
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Recommit test: would we buy it today if we did not own it.

quote: If there's a third shortfall, the typical process is to say, let's shift analyst coverage.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Third shortfall step.

quote: So it's explicitly part of our compensation process how other analysts rank order the rest of the team in terms of how helpful they've been.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Peer ranking of helpfulness is part of pay.

quote: our belief that eventually stock prices and business values have to come together and that we are invested with management teams that will be proactive about making that happen.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: How he handles being out of sync with the market.

quote: So, if we're right on our forecast, if we're right in our belief of what a business is worth and what it's going to be worth at some point in time, the swings up and down in the interim, uh, if anything, are an opportunity for the management maybe to repurchase shares more cheaply
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Price swings are chances for buybacks and acquisitions.

quote: this is our time to shine. These are the periods we tend to add value in.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Email to staff days after Liberation Day 2025 (market fall).

quote: you go out uh shopping and you see which clothes are on the sales rack or overstocked rack.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Everyday life as a source of ideas.

quote: Under Armour was the only store that still had most of the merchandise left in the store.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: After Chicago riots; read as a sign of brand strength.

quote: everything you do from stories your kids tell you to grocery shopping to reading the newspaper, you're always thinking about is there an investment angle for something that I'm learning about today.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Idea sourcing from daily life.

quote: we acknowledge that GAP accounting was really constructed for a tangible world.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Reason to recast statements for intangibles.

quote: we went through the income statement and said, "Where's the disconnect? Why is private equity seeing value here when you can't see any of it reflected in net income?
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Cable TV, early years: private equity paid about 10 times EBITDA while book value and earnings were negative.

quote: we changed the accounting on those to more replicate realworld decay of those assets.
speaker: Bill Nygren
measure: earnings adjusted for real asset life
note: Cable: plant depreciated over 5 years, ~50 years real life; customer acquisition cost expensed.

quote: We owned Amgen, one of the largest biotech companies in the early 80s when we looked at what's the enterprise value divided by pre-R&D cash flow and it was cheaper than the traditional pharmaceutical companies on that metric
speaker: Bill Nygren
measure: enterprise value to pre-R&D cash flow
note: Amgen: recast R&D as investment.

quote: It's getting to be a higher and higher percentage of our companies that we need to recast the income statement and balance sheet to better reflect real world economics.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Recasting of R&D, advertising, sales spend and customer acquisition.

quote: it struck us that on a per subscriber basis, it was selling at less than half of what HBO was.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Netflix versus HBO.

quote: we we bought it on the belief that their subs should be valued more like cable TV subs.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Netflix valued as cable subs at about $1,000 each; stock at about six times the yearly addition of value.

quote: We were looking at it saying it sells at about six times the annual increment of value that they're adding to their base business value.
speaker: Bill Nygren
measure: price to annual increment in subscriber value
note: Netflix, market cap near $150 billion then.

quote: we'll set a sell target that depending on the riskiness of the business, the balance sheet, etc.
speaker: Bill Nygren
measure: sell target relative to business value
note: Sell target set at entry.

quote: they make their best estimate of what the company can earn over the next seven years and then we discount that back and we're looking to buy at a discount
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Analyst recommendation basis.

quote: be somewhere between 85 and 95% of our guess of what the true business value of the company is today.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Sell target range, depending on riskiness.

quote: the analyst job is to respond to all new information and make sure their estimate of business value reflects everything we know up till that moment, not just what we knew at the time when they recommended the stock.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Estimates updated continuously.

quote: So again, I said our typical holding period's about 5 years.
speaker: Bill Nygren

quote: We would expect most of the companies we own to be growing business value something like 8 to 10% a year.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Implies sell target about 50% above buy value over the hold.

quote: We try to discourage that and we prize accuracy. And the whole path of when we start buying a stock until we sell it is trying to squeeze out any conservatism in our numbers and make sure we're selling on our true best guess, most accurate estimate of value.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: He says most value investors pride themselves on conservatism; Harris does not.

quote: our belief is if a stock attains that to continue owning that stock rather than recycling that capital into another that's at 60% of what we think it's worth would be hurting our expected return.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Sell at target and recycle into a name at about 60% of value.

quote: Using sell targets didn't prevent us from owning Apple for 12 years.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Apple bought about 2009, sold around 2021, about 30 times the money.

quote: it was the analyst diligently updating every quarter, making sure that the new sell target reflected all the growth that had exceeded our expectations.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Lesson: raise the sell target with new information rather than hold without a target.

quote: We didn't buy the stock thinking we'd make tens of times our capital on it. We bought it thinking it was selling at twothirds of value.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Apple entry.

quote: to me, the idea that you buy these highquality businesses and never ever reassess and just hold them kind of turns you into a momentum investor.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Against buy and hold with no sell target.

quote: once something passes an estimate of business value, then you're either you haven't properly accounted for everything in that business value or you're playing somewhat of a greater fool game.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Why he sells above value.

quote: always trying to hire people that are ethical and hardworking and smarter than we are
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Hiring approach.

quote: You know when I started just buying low PE stocks or low price to book stocks and being patient was a winning formula.
speaker: Bill Nygren
measure: price to earnings, price to book
note: His early career, before the data became easy to screen.

quote: First, you can replicate them at almost no cost with a value factor fund, but second, it's not that effective anymore.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: On managers who still buy simple low PE or low price to book.

quote: as information becomes easy to access and is therefore ubiquitous is it stops having its ability to add value. So our approach has had to evolve kind of to stay ahead of what you could computerize.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Why Harris moved beyond screens.

quote: So, I think trying to make sure that your process is staying ahead of what can be done passively uh is also a very important part of of our success.
speaker: Bill Nygren

quote: having a discipline that everyone on the team buys into and having everyone on the team believe that if the team is successful that's their personal path to how it will be most economically beneficial to them as an individual.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: His answer on what is replicable at Harris.

quote: it's very difficult to be a one-man show and be successful for any extended period of time.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Team approach.

quote: how much more important momentum is to so many investors processes today. And I think that's true.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: A reason value has been out of favour for a decade.

quote: equally important has been the acceleration of growth that we've seen in very very large companies.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: The second reason value lagged.

quote: part of what value investing depends on is that the most successful companies today because they have such high returns on capital are going to invite competition.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Mean reversion of high returns.

quote: we've never seen such issue specific or industry specific concentration in the S&P 500. It's effectively become a concentrated meggaap growth fund.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: Index concentration in 2025.

quote: It it's kind of a bet that capitalism didn't work and I'm not going to make that bet.
speaker: Bill Nygren
note: On betting that the largest growth companies keep growing for 25 years.
